# gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/

## Expand description

Project site is [here](https://gtk-rs.org/).

**Rust** bindings and wrappers for [GDK 3](https://developer.gnome.org/gdk3/),
part of [gtk3-rs](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs).

GDK **3.18** is the lowest supported version for the underlying library.

Currently, the minimum supported Rust version is `1.56.0`.

We recommend using [crates from crates.io](https://crates.io/keywords/gtk-rs),
as [demonstrated here](https://gtk-rs.org/#using).

If you want to track the bleeding edge, use the git dependency instead:

```
[dependencies]
gdk = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs.git", package = "gdk" }
```
Avoid mixing versioned and git crates like this:

```
[dependencies]
gdk = "0.13"
gdk = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs.git", package = "gdk" }
```
**gdk** is available under the MIT License, please refer to it.

GdkAppLaunchContext is an implementation of [ gio::AppLaunchContext](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/gio/auto/app_launch_context/struct.AppLaunchContext.html) that
handles launching an application in a graphical context. It provides
startup notification and allows to launch applications on a specific
screen or workspace.

In addition to a single pointer and keyboard for user interface input, GDK contains support for a variety of input devices, including graphics tablets, touchscreens and multiple pointers/keyboards interacting simultaneously with the user interface. Such input devices often have additional features, such as sub-pixel positioning information and additional device-dependent information.

Used for button press and button release events. The
`type` field will be one of [ EventType::ButtonPress](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ButtonPress),
[

`EventType::_2buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_2buttonPress], [`EventType::_3buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_3buttonPress] or [,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ButtonRelease)

`EventType::ButtonRelease`Generated when a pointer or keyboard grab is broken. On X11, this happens
when the grab window becomes unviewable (i.e. it or one of its ancestors
is unmapped), or if the same application grabs the pointer or keyboard
again. Note that implicit grabs (which are initiated by button presses)
can also cause [ EventGrabBroken](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventGrabBroken.html) events.

Generated when the owner of a selection changes. On X11, this information is only available if the X server supports the XFIXES extension.

Proximity events are generated when using GDK’s wrapper for the XInput extension. The XInput extension is an add-on for standard X that allows you to use nonstandard devices such as graphics tablets. A proximity event indicates that the stylus has moved in or out of contact with the tablet, or perhaps that the user’s finger has moved in or out of contact with a touch screen.

Generated from button presses for the buttons 4 to 7. Wheel mice are usually configured to generate button press events for buttons 4 and 5 when the wheel is turned.

Generated when a selection is requested or ownership of a selection is taken over by another client application.

A [ FrameClock](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.FrameClock.html) tells the application when to update and repaint a
window. This may be synced to the vertical refresh rate of the
monitor, for example. Even when the frame clock uses a simple timer
rather than a hardware-based vertical sync, the frame clock helps
because it ensures everything paints at the same time (reducing the
total number of frames). The frame clock can also automatically
stop painting when it knows the frames will not be visible, or
scale back animation framerates.

A [ FrameTimings](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.FrameTimings.html) object holds timing information for a single frame
of the application’s displays. To retrieve

[objects, use](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.FrameTimings.html)

`FrameTimings`[or](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.FrameClock.html#method.timings)

`FrameClock::timings()`[. The information in](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.FrameClock.html#method.current_timings)

`FrameClock::current_timings()`[is useful for precise synchronization of video with the event or audio streams, and for measuring quality metrics for the application’s display, such as latency and jitter.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.FrameTimings.html)

`FrameTimings`A [ Keymap](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Keymap.html) defines the translation from keyboard state
(including a hardware key, a modifier mask, and active keyboard group)
to a keyval. This translation has two phases. The first phase is
to determine the effective keyboard group and level for the keyboard
state; the second phase is to look up the keycode/group/level triplet
in the keymap and see what keyval it corresponds to.

A set of bit-flags to indicate the state of modifier keys and mouse buttons in various event types. Typical modifier keys are Shift, Control, Meta, Super, Hyper, Alt, Compose, Apple, CapsLock or ShiftLock.

# gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/index.html

## Expand description

Project site is [here](https://gtk-rs.org/).

**Rust** bindings and wrappers for [GDK 3](https://developer.gnome.org/gdk3/),
part of [gtk3-rs](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs).

GDK **3.18** is the lowest supported version for the underlying library.

Currently, the minimum supported Rust version is `1.56.0`.

We recommend using [crates from crates.io](https://crates.io/keywords/gtk-rs),
as [demonstrated here](https://gtk-rs.org/#using).

If you want to track the bleeding edge, use the git dependency instead:

```
[dependencies]
gdk = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs.git", package = "gdk" }
```
Avoid mixing versioned and git crates like this:

```
[dependencies]
gdk = "0.13"
gdk = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs.git", package = "gdk" }
```
**gdk** is available under the MIT License, please refer to it.

# Unlocking the GNOME stack for Rust – gtk-rs

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/

#

          Unlocking the GNOME stack for Rust [§](https://gtk-rs.org#unlocking-the-gnome-stack-for-rust)

The **gtk-rs** project provides safe bindings to the [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org) language for fundamental libraries from the [GNOME](https://developer.gnome.org/components/) stack like [GLib](https://developer.gnome.org/glib), [Cairo](https://cairographics.org/documentation/), and [GTK 4](https://gtk.org).

##

          Available crates [§](https://gtk-rs.org#available-crates)

The following table contains the most popular crates of **gtk-rs**. More information on all existing crates is available under the corresponding links in the **Project** column in the table below.

| Project | Crate | Docs | |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Core](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core) | [
        cairo-rs
      ](https://crates.io/crates/cairo-rs) | [

      ](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/cairo) | |
| [
    ](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core) | [
        gio
      ](https://crates.io/crates/gio) | [

      ](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/latest/docs/gio) | |
| [
    ](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core) | [
        glib
      ](https://crates.io/crates/glib) | [

      ](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk4-rs/stable/latest/docs/gtk4) | |

##

          The introductory book [§](https://gtk-rs.org#the-introductory-book)

  Julian Hofer is writing a book titled [GUI development with Rust and GTK 4](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk4-rs/stable/latest/book). We recommend both new and experienced **gtk-rs** users to have a look at it. While this book is targeted at people who want to develop GTK 4 applications, it also covers more general aspects of the GNOME stack such as **GObject Concepts**, **The Main Event Loop** and **GSettings**.

##

          The gtk-rs ecosystem [§](https://gtk-rs.org#the-gtk-rs-ecosystem)

By now, a number of additional bindings for GObject based libraries exist. While not part of the gtk-rs project, many of them are developed in close collaboration. Notable other projects within the gtk-rs ecosystem are

- **GStreamer**Open source multimedia framework
- **Adwaita**Building blocks for modern GNOME applications
- **SourceView 5**A library extending GtkTextView with features typical for a source code editor
- **Relm 4**An idiomatic GUI library inspired by Elm and based on gtk4-rs

More bindings can be found as part of the [GNOME GitLab Rust Group](https://gitlab.gnome.org/World/Rust).

All these bindings are generated on the basis of GObject introspection (GIR). The book [Generate Rust bindings for GIR based libraries](https://gtk-rs.org/gir/book/) provides the documentation for the tools that gtk-rs provides to generate such bindings.

          Apps built with gtk-rs [§](https://gtk-rs.org#apps-built-with-gtk-rs)

# gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/git/docs/gdk

## Expand description

Project site is [here](https://gtk-rs.org/).

**Rust** bindings and wrappers for [GDK 3](https://developer.gnome.org/gdk3/),
part of [gtk3-rs](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs).

GDK **3.22** is the lowest supported version for the underlying library.

Currently, the minimum supported Rust version is `1.63.0`.

We recommend using [crates from crates.io](https://crates.io/keywords/gtk-rs),
as [demonstrated here](https://gtk-rs.org/#using).

If you want to track the bleeding edge, use the git dependency instead:

```
[dependencies]
gdk = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs.git", package = "gdk" }
```
Avoid mixing versioned and git crates like this:

```
[dependencies]
gdk = "0.13"
gdk = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk3-rs.git", package = "gdk" }
```
**gdk** is available under the MIT License, please refer to it.

# cairo - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/cairo/index.html

## Expand description

**Rust** bindings for Rust and wrappers for [Cairo](https://www.cairographics.org/), part of [gtk-rs-core](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core).

Cairo **1.14** is the lowest supported version for the underlying library.

Currently, the minimum supported Rust version is `1.56.0`.

- **use_glib**- Use with- [glib](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/index.html)

- **png**- Reading and writing PNG images
- **pdf**- Rendering PDF documents
- **svg**- Rendering SVG documents
- **ps**- Rendering PostScript documents

- **v1_16**- Use Cairo 1.16 APIs

- **dox**- Used to keep system dependent items in documentation

- **xcb**- X Window System rendering using the XCB library
- **xlib**- X Window System rendering using XLib

- **win32-surface**- Microsoft Windows surface support

We recommend using [crates from crates.io](https://crates.io/keywords/gtk-rs),
as [demonstrated here](https://gtk-rs.org/#using).

If you want to track the bleeding edge, use the git dependency instead:

```
[dependencies]
cairo-rs = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core.git", package = "cairo-rs" }
```
Avoid mixing versioned and git crates like this:

```
# This will not compile
[dependencies]
cairo-rs = "0.13"
cairo-rs = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core.git", package = "cairo-rs" }
```
**cairo** is available under the MIT License, please refer to it.

- `pub use ffi;`
- `pub use freetype_crate as freetype;`

- Resets all static data within cairo to its original state (i.e. identical to the state at program invocation). For example, all caches within cairo will be flushed empty.

# gdk_pixbuf - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/gdk_pixbuf/index.html

## Expand description

**Rust** bindings and wrappers for [GDK-Pixbuf](https://docs.gtk.org/gdk-pixbuf), part of [gtk-rs-core](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core).

GDK-PixBuf **2.32** is the lowest supported version for the underlying library.

Currently, the minimum supported Rust version is `1.56.0`.

We recommend using [crates from crates.io](https://crates.io/keywords/gtk-rs),
as [demonstrated here](https://gtk-rs.org/#using).

If you want to track the bleeding edge, use the git dependency instead:

```
[dependencies]
gdk-pixbuf = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core.git", package = "gdk-pixbuf" }
```
Avoid mixing versioned and git crates like this:

```
# This will not compile
[dependencies]
gdk-pixbuf = "0.13"
gdk-pixbuf = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core.git", package = "gdk-pixbuf" }
```
**gdk-pixbuf** is available under the MIT License, please refer to it.

- Traits intended for blanket imports.

- A pixel buffer.
- An opaque object representing an animation.
- An opaque object representing an iterator which points to a certain position in an animation.
- Flags which allow a module to specify further details about the supported operations.
- Incremental image loader.
- Implements
- An opaque struct representing a simple animation.

- This enumeration defines the color spaces that are supported by the gdk-pixbuf library.
- Interpolation modes for scaling functions.
- Control the alpha channel for drawables.
- An error code in the`GDK_PIXBUF_ERROR`domain.
- The possible rotations which can be passed to gdk_pixbuf_rotate_simple().

# glib - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/index.html

## Expand description

**Rust** bindings and wrappers for [GLib](https://docs.gtk.org/glib/), part of [gtk-rs-core](https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core).

GLib **2.48** is the lowest supported version for the underlying library.

This library contains bindings to GLib and GObject types and APIs as well as common building blocks used in both handmade and machine generated bindings to GTK and other GLib-based libraries.

It is the foundation for higher level libraries with uniform Rusty (safe and strongly typed) APIs. It avoids exposing GLib-specific data types where possible and is not meant to provide comprehensive GLib bindings, which would often amount to duplicating the Rust Standard Library or other utility crates.

Currently, the minimum supported Rust version is `1.56.0`.

Most types in the GLib family have [ Type](https://gtk-rs.org/types/struct.Type.html) identifiers.
Their corresponding Rust types implement the

[trait.](https://gtk-rs.org/types/trait.StaticType.html)

`StaticType`A dynamically typed [ Value](https://gtk-rs.org/value/struct.Value.html) can carry values of any

[.](https://gtk-rs.org/types/trait.StaticType.html)

`StaticType`[s can carry values of](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/struct.Variant.html)

`Variant`[.](https://gtk-rs.org/variant/trait.StaticVariantType.html)

`StaticVariantType`Errors are represented by [ Error](https://gtk-rs.org/error/struct.Error.html), which can
carry values from various

[error domains](https://gtk-rs.org/error/trait.ErrorDomain.html)such as

[.](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.FileError.html)

`FileError`Each class and interface has a corresponding smart pointer struct
representing an instance of that type (e.g. [ Object](https://gtk-rs.org/object/struct.Object.html) for

`GObject` or
`gtk::Widget` for `GtkWidget`). They are reference counted and feature
interior mutability similarly to Rust’s `Rc<RefCell<T>>` idiom.
Consequently, cloning objects is cheap and their methods never require
mutable borrows. Two smart pointers are equal if they point to the same
object.The root of the object hierarchy is [ Object](https://gtk-rs.org/object/struct.Object.html).
Inheritance and subtyping is denoted with the

[marker trait. The](https://gtk-rs.org/object/trait.IsA.html)

`IsA`[trait enables upcasting and downcasting.](https://gtk-rs.org/object/trait.Cast.html)

`Cast`Interfaces and non-leaf classes also have corresponding traits (e.g.
[ ObjectExt](https://gtk-rs.org/object/trait.ObjectExt.html) or

`gtk::WidgetExt`), which are blanketly implemented for all
their subtypes.You can create new subclasses of [ Object](https://gtk-rs.org/object/struct.Object.html) or other object types. Look at
the module’s documentation for further details and a code example.

GLib-based libraries largely operate on pointers to various boxed or
reference counted structures so the bindings have to implement corresponding
smart pointers (wrappers), which encapsulate resource management and safety
checks. Such wrappers are defined via the
[ wrapper](https://gtk-rs.org/macro.wrapper.html) macro, which uses abstractions
defined in the

[,](https://gtk-rs.org/wrapper/index.html)

`wrapper`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/boxed/index.html)

`boxed`[and](https://gtk-rs.org/shared/index.html)

`shared`[modules.](https://gtk-rs.org/object/index.html)

`object`The [ translate](https://gtk-rs.org/translate/index.html) module defines and partly implements
conversions between high level Rust types (including the aforementioned
wrappers) and their FFI counterparts.

We recommend using [crates from crates.io](https://crates.io/keywords/gtk-rs),
as [demonstrated here](https://gtk-rs.org/#using).

If you want to track the bleeding edge, use the git dependency instead:

```
[dependencies]
glib = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core.git", package = "glib" }
```
Avoid mixing versioned and git crates like this:

```
# This will not compile
[dependencies]
glib = "0.13"
glib = { git = "https://github.com/gtk-rs/gtk-rs-core.git", package = "glib" }
```
**glib** is available under the MIT License, please refer to it.

# AnchorHints in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.AnchorHints.html

`pub struct AnchorHints { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`v3_22`## Expand description

Positioning hints for aligning a window relative to a rectangle.

These hints determine how the window should be positioned in the case that the window would fall off-screen if placed in its ideal position.

For example, [ FLIP_X](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.AnchorHints.html#associatedconstant.FLIP_X) will replace

[with](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.Gravity.html#variant.NorthWest)

`Gravity::NorthWest`[and vice versa if the window extends beyond the left or right edges of the monitor.](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.Gravity.html#variant.NorthEast)

`Gravity::NorthEast`If [ SLIDE_X](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.AnchorHints.html#associatedconstant.SLIDE_X) is set, the window can be shifted horizontally to fit
on-screen. If

[is set, the window can be shrunken horizontally to fit.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.AnchorHints.html#associatedconstant.RESIZE_X)

`RESIZE_X`In general, when multiple flags are set, flipping should take precedence over sliding, which should take precedence over resizing.

# AppLaunchContext in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.AppLaunchContext.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct AppLaunchContext { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

GdkAppLaunchContext is an implementation of [ gio::AppLaunchContext](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/gio/auto/app_launch_context/struct.AppLaunchContext.html) that
handles launching an application in a graphical context. It provides
startup notification and allows to launch applications on a specific
screen or workspace.

**⚠️ The following code is in C ⚠️**

```
GdkAppLaunchContext *context;
context = gdk_display_get_app_launch_context (display);
gdk_app_launch_context_set_screen (screen);
gdk_app_launch_context_set_timestamp (event->time);
if (!g_app_info_launch_default_for_uri ("http://www.gtk.org", context, &error))
  g_warning ("Launching failed: %s\n", error->message);
g_object_unref (context);
```

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

Returns the intersection between the flags in `self` and
`other`.

Specifically, the returned set contains only the flags which are
present in *both* `self` *and* `other`.

This is equivalent to using the `&` operator (e.g.
[ ops::BitAnd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.BitAnd.html)), as in

`flags & other`.Returns the union of between the flags in `self` and `other`.

#### pub const fn [difference](https://gtk-rs.org#method.difference)(self, other: Self) -> Self

Returns the difference between the flags in `self` and `other`.

Specifically, the returned set contains all flags present in
`self`, except for the ones present in `other`.

It is also conceptually equivalent to the “bit-clear” operation:
`flags & !other` (and this syntax is also supported).

This is equivalent to using the `-` operator (e.g.
[ ops::Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Sub.html)), as in

`flags - other`.[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/flags.rs.html#134-167)#### pub const fn [symmetric_difference](https://gtk-rs.org#method.symmetric_difference)(self, other: Self) -> Self

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/flags.rs.html#134-167)

#### pub const fn [symmetric_difference](https://gtk-rs.org#method.symmetric_difference)(self, other: Self) -> Self

Returns the [symmetric difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_difference) between the flags
in `self` and `other`.

Specifically, the returned set contains the flags present which
are present in `self` or `other`, but that are not present in
both. Equivalently, it contains the flags present in *exactly
one* of the sets `self` and `other`.

This is equivalent to using the `^` operator (e.g.

#### pub const fn [complement](https://gtk-rs.org#method.complement)(self) -> Self

Returns the complement of this set of flags.

Specifically, the returned set contains all the flags which are
not set in `self`, but which are allowed for this type.

Alternatively, it can be thought of as the set difference
between [ Self::all()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.AxisFlags.html#method.all) and

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

# Device in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.Device.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct Device { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [ Device](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html) object represents a single input device, such
as a keyboard, a mouse, a touchpad, etc.

See the [ DeviceManager](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DeviceManager.html) documentation for more information
about the various kinds of master and slave devices, and their
relationships.

This is an Abstract Base Class, you cannot instantiate it.

`GSettings` paths to store settings for this device.**⚠️ The following code is in C ⚠️**

```
 static GSettings *
 get_device_settings (GdkDevice *device)
 {
   const gchar *vendor, *product;
   GSettings *settings;
   GdkDevice *device;
   gchar *path;
   vendor = gdk_device_get_vendor_id (device);
   product = gdk_device_get_product_id (device);
   path = g_strdup_printf ("/org/example/app/devices/%s:%s/", vendor, product);
   settings = g_settings_new_with_path (DEVICE_SCHEMA, path);
   g_free (path);
   return settings;
 }
```

#### pub fn [grab](https://gtk-rs.org#method.grab)(

    &self,

    window: &[Window](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html),

    grab_ownership: [GrabOwnership](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.GrabOwnership.html),

    owner_events: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),

    event_mask: [EventMask](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventMask.html),

    cursor: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&[Cursor](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Cursor.html)>,

    time_: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

) -> [GrabStatus](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.GrabStatus.html)

Grabs the device so that all events coming from this device are passed to
this application until the device is ungrabbed with [ ungrab()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html#method.ungrab),
or the window becomes unviewable. This overrides any previous grab on the device
by this client.

Note that `self` and `window` need to be on the same display.

Device grabs are used for operations which need complete control over the given device events (either pointer or keyboard). For example in GTK+ this is used for Drag and Drop operations, popup menus and such.

Note that if the event mask of an X window has selected both button press
and button release events, then a button press event will cause an automatic
pointer grab until the button is released. X does this automatically since
most applications expect to receive button press and release events in pairs.
It is equivalent to a pointer grab on the window with `owner_events` set to
[ true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html).

If you set up anything at the time you take the grab that needs to be
cleaned up when the grab ends, you should handle the [ EventGrabBroken](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventGrabBroken.html)
events that are emitted when the grab ends unvoluntarily.

Use [ Seat::grab()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Seat.html#method.grab) instead.

the [ Window](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html) which will own the grab (the grab window)

specifies the grab ownership.

if [ false](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) then all device events are reported with respect to

`window` and are only reported if selected by `event_mask`. If
[then pointer events for this application are reported as normal, but pointer events outside this application are reported with respect to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`true``window` and only if selected by
`event_mask`. In either mode, unreported events are discarded.specifies the event mask, which is used in accordance with
`owner_events`.

the cursor to display while the grab is active if the device is
a pointer. If this is [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) then the normal cursors are used for

`window` and its descendants, and the cursor for `window` is used
elsewhere.the timestamp of the event which led to this pointer grab. This
usually comes from the `GdkEvent` struct, though `GDK_CURRENT_TIME`
can be used if the time isn’t known.

[ GrabStatus::Success](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.GrabStatus.html#variant.Success) if the grab was successful.

Obtains the motion history for a pointer device; given a starting and
ending timestamp, return all events in the motion history for
the device in the given range of time. Some windowing systems
do not support motion history, in which case, [ false](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) will
be returned. (This is not distinguishable from the case where
motion history is supported and no events were found.)

Note that there is also [ Window::set_event_compression()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.set_event_compression) to get

#### fn [dynamic_cast](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.Cast.html#method.dynamic_cast)<T>(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, Self> where

    T: [ObjectType](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectType.html),

Tries to cast to an object of type `T`. This handles upcasting, downcasting
and casting between interface and interface implementors. All checks are performed at
runtime, while `downcast` and `upcast` will do many checks at compile-time already. [Read more](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.Cast.html#method.dynamic_cast)

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

[Read more](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)

# DeviceManager in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.DeviceManager.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct DeviceManager { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

In addition to a single pointer and keyboard for user interface input, GDK contains support for a variety of input devices, including graphics tablets, touchscreens and multiple pointers/keyboards interacting simultaneously with the user interface. Such input devices often have additional features, such as sub-pixel positioning information and additional device-dependent information.

In order to query the device hierarchy and be aware of changes in the
device hierarchy (such as virtual devices being created or removed, or
physical devices being plugged or unplugged), GDK provides
[ DeviceManager](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DeviceManager.html).

By default, and if the platform supports it, GDK is aware of multiple
keyboard/pointer pairs and multitouch devices. This behavior can be
changed by calling `gdk_disable_multidevice()` before [ Display::open()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Display.html#method.open).
There should rarely be a need to do that though, since GDK defaults
to a compatibility mode in which it will emit just one enter/leave
event pair for all devices on a window. To enable per-device
enter/leave events and other multi-pointer interaction features,

[must be called on](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.set_support_multidevice)

`Window::set_support_multidevice()``GdkWindows` (or `gtk_widget_set_support_multidevice()` on widgets).
window. See the [documentation for more information.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.set_support_multidevice)

`Window::set_support_multidevice()`On X11, multi-device support is implemented through XInput 2.
Unless `gdk_disable_multidevice()` is called, the XInput 2
[ DeviceManager](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DeviceManager.html) implementation will be used as the input source.
Otherwise either the core or XInput 1 implementations will be used.

For simple applications that don’t have any special interest in
input devices, the so-called “client pointer”
provides a reasonable approximation to a simple setup with a single
pointer and keyboard. The device that has been set as the client
pointer can be accessed via [ client_pointer()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DeviceManager.html#method.client_pointer).

Conceptually, in multidevice mode there are 2 device types. Virtual devices (or master devices) are represented by the pointer cursors and keyboard foci that are seen on the screen. Physical devices (or slave devices) represent the hardware that is controlling the virtual devices, and thus have no visible cursor on the screen.

Virtual devices are always paired, so there is a keyboard device for every
pointer device. Associations between devices may be inspected through
[ Device::associated_device()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html#method.associated_device).

There may be several virtual devices, and several physical devices could be controlling each of these virtual devices. Physical devices may also be “floating”, which means they are not attached to any virtual device.

```
carlos@sacarino:~$ xinput list
⎡ Virtual core pointer                          id=2    [master pointer  (3)]
⎜   ↳ Virtual core XTEST pointer                id=4    [slave  pointer  (2)]
⎜   ↳ Wacom ISDv4 E6 Pen stylus                 id=10   [slave  pointer  (2)]
⎜   ↳ Wacom ISDv4 E6 Finger touch               id=11   [slave  pointer  (2)]
⎜   ↳ SynPS/2 Synaptics TouchPad                id=13   [slave  pointer  (2)]
⎜   ↳ TPPS/2 IBM TrackPoint                     id=14   [slave  pointer  (2)]
⎜   ↳ Wacom ISDv4 E6 Pen eraser                 id=16   [slave  pointer  (2)]
⎣ Virtual core keyboard                         id=3    [master keyboard (2)]
    ↳ Virtual core XTEST keyboard               id=5    [slave  keyboard (3)]
    ↳ Power Button                              id=6    [slave  keyboard (3)]
    ↳ Video Bus                                 id=7    [slave  keyboard (3)]
    ↳ Sleep Button                              id=8    [slave  keyboard (3)]
    ↳ Integrated Camera                         id=9    [slave  keyboard (3)]
    ↳ AT Translated Set 2 keyboard              id=12   [slave  keyboard (3)]
    ↳ ThinkPad Extra Buttons                    id=15   [slave  keyboard (3)]
```
By default, GDK will automatically listen for events coming from all
master devices, setting the [ Device](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html) for all events coming from input
devices. Events containing device information are

[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.MotionNotify)

`EventType::MotionNotify`[, [](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ButtonPress)

`EventType::ButtonPress``EventType::_2buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_2buttonPress], [`EventType::_3buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_3buttonPress],
[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ButtonRelease)

`EventType::ButtonRelease`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.Scroll)

`EventType::Scroll`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.KeyPress)

`EventType::KeyPress`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.KeyRelease)

`EventType::KeyRelease`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.EnterNotify)

`EventType::EnterNotify`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.LeaveNotify)

`EventType::LeaveNotify`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.FocusChange)

`EventType::FocusChange`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ProximityIn)

`EventType::ProximityIn`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ProximityOut)

`EventType::ProximityOut`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.DragEnter)

`EventType::DragEnter`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.DragLeave)

`EventType::DragLeave`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.DragMotion)

`EventType::DragMotion`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.DragStatus)

`EventType::DragStatus`[,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.DropStart)

`EventType::DropStart`[and](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.DropFinished)

`EventType::DropFinished`[. When dealing with an event on a master device, it is possible to get the source (slave) device that the event originated from via](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.GrabBroken)

`EventType::GrabBroken``gdk_event_get_source_device()`.On a standard session, all physical devices are connected by default to the “Virtual Core Pointer/Keyboard” master devices, hence routing all events through these. This behavior is only modified by device grabs, where the slave device is temporarily detached for as long as the grab is held, and more permanently by user modifications to the device hierarchy.

On certain application specific setups, it may make sense
to detach a physical device from its master pointer, and mapping it to
an specific window. This can be achieved by the combination of
[ Device::grab()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html#method.grab) and

[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html#method.set_mode)

`Device::set_mode()`In order to listen for events coming from devices
other than a virtual device, [ Window::set_device_events()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.set_device_events) must be
called. Generally, this function can be used to modify the event mask
for any given device.

Input devices may also provide additional information besides X/Y.
For example, graphics tablets may also provide pressure and X/Y tilt
information. This information is device-dependent, and may be
queried through `gdk_device_get_axis()`. In multidevice mode, virtual
devices will change axes in order to always represent the physical
device that is routing events through it. Whenever the physical device
changes, the `property::Device::n-axes` property will be notified, and
[ Device::list_axes()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html#method.list_axes) will return the new device axes.

Devices may also have associated “keys” or
macro buttons. Such keys can be globally set to map into normal X
keyboard events. The mapping is set using [ Device::set_key()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html#method.set_key).

In GTK+ 3.20, a new [ Seat](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Seat.html) object has been introduced that
supersedes

[and should be preferred in newly written code.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DeviceManager.html)

`DeviceManager`This is an Abstract Base Class, you cannot instantiate it.

Returns the client pointer, that is, the master pointer that acts as the core pointer for this application. In X11, window managers may change this depending on the interaction pattern under the presence of several pointers.

You should use this function seldomly, only in code that isn’t triggered by a `GdkEvent`
and there aren’t other means to get a meaningful [ Device](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Device.html) to operate on.

Use [ Seat::pointer()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Seat.html#method.pointer) instead.

The client pointer. This memory is owned by GDK and must not be freed or unreferenced.

The ::device-changed signal is emitted whenever a device has changed in the hierarchy, either slave devices being disconnected from their master device or connected to another one, or master devices being added or removed a slave device.

If a slave device is detached from all master devices

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

[Read more](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)

# DevicePad in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.DevicePad.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct DevicePad { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

[ DevicePad](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DevicePad.html) is an interface implemented by devices of type

[, it allows querying the features provided by the pad device.](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.InputSource.html#variant.TabletPad)

`InputSource::TabletPad`Tablet pads may contain one or more groups, each containing a subset
of the buttons/rings/strips available. [ DevicePadExt::n_groups()](https://gtk-rs.org/prelude/trait.DevicePadExt.html#tymethod.n_groups)
can be used to obtain the number of groups,

[and](https://gtk-rs.org/prelude/trait.DevicePadExt.html#tymethod.n_features)

`DevicePadExt::n_features()`[can be combined to find out the number of buttons/rings/strips the device has, and how are they grouped.](https://gtk-rs.org/prelude/trait.DevicePadExt.html#tymethod.feature_group)

`DevicePadExt::feature_group()`Each of those groups have different modes, which may be used to map
each individual pad feature to multiple actions. Only one mode is
effective (current) for each given group, different groups may have
different current modes. The number of available modes in a group can
be found out through [ DevicePadExt::group_n_modes()](https://gtk-rs.org/prelude/trait.DevicePadExt.html#tymethod.group_n_modes), and the current
mode for a given group will be notified through the

[event.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventPadGroupMode.html)

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

[Read more](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)

## Expand description

An enumeration describing the type of an input device in general terms.

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

Non-exhaustive enums could have additional variants added in future. Therefore, when matching against variants of non-exhaustive enums, an extra wildcard arm must be added to account for any future variants.

the device is a mouse. (This will be reported for the core

the device is an eraser. Typically, this would be the other end
of a stylus on a graphics tablet.

the device is a graphics tablet “puck” or similar device.

the device is a keyboard.

the device is a direct-input touch device, such
as a touchscreen or tablet. This device type has been added in 3.4.

the device is an indirect touch device, such
as a touchpad. This device type has been added in 3.4.

the device is a “pad”, a collection of buttons,
rings and strips found in drawing tablets. This device type has been
added in 3.22.

`v3_22`Gets the hardware ID of this tool, or 0 if it’s not known. When
non-zero, the identificator is unique for the given tool model,
meaning that two identical tools will share the same `hardware_id`,
but will have different serial numbers (see [ serial()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DeviceTool.html#method.serial)).

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

[Read more](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)

# Display in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.Display.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct Display { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

[ Display](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Display.html) objects purpose are two fold:

-
To manage and provide information about input devices (pointers and keyboards)
-
To manage and provide information about the available `GdkScreens`

GdkDisplay objects are the GDK representation of an X Display, which can be described as a workstation consisting of a keyboard, a pointing device (such as a mouse) and one or more screens. It is used to open and keep track of various GdkScreen objects currently instantiated by the application. It is also used to access the keyboard(s) and mouse pointer(s) of the display.

Most of the input device handling has been factored out into
the separate [ DeviceManager](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DeviceManager.html) object. Every display has a
device manager, which you can obtain using

[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Display.html#method.device_manager)

`device_manager()`Closes the connection to the windowing system for the given display, and cleans up associated resources.

Flushes any requests queued for the windowing system; this happens automatically when the main loop blocks waiting for new events, but if your application is drawing without returning control to the main loop, you may need to call this function explicitly. A common case where this function needs to be called is when an application is executing drawing commands from a thread other than the thread where the main loop is running.

This is most useful for X11. On windowing systems where requests are handled synchronously, this function will do nothing.

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

# DisplayManager in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.DisplayManager.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct DisplayManager { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The purpose of the [ DisplayManager](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DisplayManager.html) singleton object is to offer
notification when displays appear or disappear or the default display
changes.

You can use [ get()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DisplayManager.html#method.get) to obtain the

[singleton, but that should be rarely necessary. Typically, initializing GTK+ opens a display that you can work with without ever accessing the](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DisplayManager.html)

`DisplayManager`[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DisplayManager.html)

`DisplayManager`The GDK library can be built with support for multiple backends.
The [ DisplayManager](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DisplayManager.html) object determines which backend is used
at runtime.

When writing backend-specific code that is supposed to work with
multiple GDK backends, you have to consider both compile time and
runtime. At compile time, use the `GDK_WINDOWING_X11`, `GDK_WINDOWING_WIN32`
macros, etc. to find out which backends are present in the GDK library
you are building your application against. At runtime, use type-check
macros like GDK_IS_X11_DISPLAY() to find out which backend is in use:

**⚠️ The following code is in C ⚠️**

```
#ifdef GDK_WINDOWING_X11
  if (GDK_IS_X11_DISPLAY (display))
    {
      // make X11-specific calls here
    }
  else
#endif
#ifdef GDK_WINDOWING_QUARTZ
  if (GDK_IS_QUARTZ_DISPLAY (display))
    {
      // make Quartz-specific calls here
    }
  else
#endif
  g_error ("Unsupported GDK backend");
```

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

[Read more](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)

Means nothing, and should not be used.

Move the data, i.e. first copy it, then delete it from the source using the DELETE target of the X selection protocol.

Add a link to the data. Note that this is only useful if source and destination agree on what it means.

Special action which tells the source that the destination will do something that the source doesn’t understand.

Ask the user what to do with the data.

#### pub const fn [intersection](https://gtk-rs.org#method.intersection)(self, other: Self) -> Self

Returns the intersection between the flags in `self` and
`other`.

Specifically, the returned set contains only the flags which are
present in *both* `self` *and* `other`.

This is equivalent to using the `&` operator (e.g.
[ ops::BitAnd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.BitAnd.html)), as in

`flags & other`.Returns the union of between the flags in `self` and `other`.

Specifically, the returned set contains all flags which are
present in *either* `self` *or* `other`, including any which are
present in both (see [ Self::symmetric_difference](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DragAction.html#method.symmetric_difference) if that
is undesirable).

This is equivalent to using the `|` operator (e.g.
[ ops::BitOr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.BitOr.html)), as in

`flags | other`.[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/flags.rs.html#239-266)#### pub const fn [difference](https://gtk-rs.org#method.difference)(self, other: Self) -> Self

#### pub const fn [difference](https://gtk-rs.org#method.difference)(self, other: Self) -> Self

Returns the difference between the flags in `self` and `other`.

Specifically, the returned set contains all flags present in
`self`, except for the ones present in `other`.

It is also conceptually equivalent to the “bit-clear” operation:
`flags & !other` (and this syntax is also supported).

This is equivalent to using the `-` operator (e.g.
[ ops::Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Sub.html)), as in

`flags - other`.[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/flags.rs.html#239-266)#### pub const fn [symmetric_difference](https://gtk-rs.org#method.symmetric_difference)(self, other: Self) -> Self

#### pub const fn [symmetric_difference](https://gtk-rs.org#method.symmetric_difference)(self, other: Self) -> Self

Returns the [symmetric difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_difference) between the flags
in `self` and `other`.

Specifically, the returned set contains the flags present which
are present in `self` or `other`, but that are not present in
both. Equivalently, it contains the flags present in *exactly
one* of the sets `self` and `other`.

This is equivalent to using the `^` operator (e.g.
[ ops::BitXor](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.BitXor.html)), as in

`flags ^ other`.[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/flags.rs.html#239-266)#### pub const fn [complement](https://gtk-rs.org#method.complement)(self) -> Self

**crate feature**only.

`v3_20`Requests the drag and drop operation to be managed by `self`.
When a drag and drop operation becomes managed, the [ DragContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DragContext.html)
will internally handle all input and source-side

[events as required by the windowing system.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventDND.html)

`EventDND`Once the drag and drop operation is managed, the drag context will emit the following signals:

- The `signal::DragContext::action-changed`signal whenever the final action to be performed by the drag and drop operation changes.
- The `signal::DragContext::drop-performed`signal after the user performs the drag and drop gesture (typically by releasing the mouse button).
- The `signal::DragContext::dnd-finished`signal after the drag and drop operation concludes (after all`GdkSelection`transfers happen).
- The `signal::DragContext::cancel`signal if the drag and drop operation is finished but doesn’t happen over an accepting destination, or is cancelled through other means.

Window to use for IPC messaging/events

the actions supported by the drag source

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

[Read more](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)

# DrawingContext in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.DrawingContext.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct DrawingContext { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

[ DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html) is an object that represents the current drawing
state of a

[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html)

`Window`It’s possible to use a [ DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html) to draw on a

[via rendering API like Cairo or OpenGL.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html)

`Window`A [ DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html) can only be created by calling

[and will be valid until a call to](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_draw_frame)

`Window::begin_draw_frame()`[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_draw_frame)

`Window::end_draw_frame()`[ DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html) is available since GDK 3.22

`v3_22`Retrieves a Cairo context to be used to draw on the [ Window](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html)
that created the

[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html)

`DrawingContext`The returned context is guaranteed to be valid as long as the
[ DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html) is valid, that is between a call to

[and](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_draw_frame)

`Window::begin_draw_frame()`[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_draw_frame)

`Window::end_draw_frame()`a Cairo context to be used to draw
the contents of the [ Window](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html). The context is owned by the

[and should not be destroyed](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html)

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/window.rs.html#117-124)

#### pub fn [begin_draw_frame](https://gtk-rs.org#method.begin_draw_frame)(&self, region: &[Region](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/cairo/region/struct.Region.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html)>

**crate feature**only.

`v3_22`Indicates that you are beginning the process of redrawing `region`
on `self`, and provides you with a [ DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html).

If `self` is a top level [ Window](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html), backed by a native window
implementation, a backing store (offscreen buffer) large enough to
contain

`region` will be created. The backing store will be initialized
with the background color or background surface for `self`. Then, all
drawing operations performed on `self` will be diverted to the
backing store. When you call `gdk_window_end_frame()`, the contents of
the backing store will be copied to `self`, making it visible
on screen. Only the part of `self` contained in `region` will be
modified; that is, drawing operations are clipped to `region`.The net result of all this is to remove flicker, because the user
sees the finished product appear all at once when you call
[ end_draw_frame()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_draw_frame). If you draw to

`self` directly without
calling [, the user may see flicker as individual drawing operations are performed in sequence.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_draw_frame)

`begin_draw_frame()`When using GTK+, the widget system automatically places calls to
[ begin_draw_frame()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_draw_frame) and

[around emissions of the](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_draw_frame)

`end_draw_frame()``GtkWidget::draw` signal. That is, if you’re
drawing the contents of the widget yourself, you can assume that the
widget has a cleared background, is already set as the clip region,
and already has a backing store. Therefore in most cases, application
code in GTK does not need to call [explicitly.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_draw_frame)

`begin_draw_frame()`a Cairo region

a [ DrawingContext](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.DrawingContext.html) context that should be
used to draw the contents of the window; the returned context is owned
by GDK.

Begins a window move operation (for a toplevel window).

This function assumes that the drag is controlled by the
client pointer device, use [ begin_move_drag_for_device()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_move_drag_for_device)
to begin a drag with a different device.

the button being used to drag, or 0 for a keyboard-initiated drag

root window X coordinate of mouse click that began the drag

root window Y coordinate of mouse click that began the drag

timestamp of mouse click that began the drag

#### pub fn [begin_paint_region](https://gtk-rs.org#method.begin_paint_region)(&self, region: &[Region](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/cairo/region/struct.Region.html))

Indicates that you are beginning the process of redrawing `region`.
A backing store (offscreen buffer) large enough to contain `region`
will be created. The backing store will be initialized with the
background color or background surface for `self`. Then, all
drawing operations performed on `self` will be diverted to the
backing store. When you call [ end_paint()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_paint), the backing
store will be copied to

`self`, making it visible onscreen. Only
the part of `self` contained in `region` will be modified; that is,
drawing operations are clipped to `region`.The net result of all this is to remove flicker, because the user
sees the finished product appear all at once when you call
[ end_paint()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_paint). If you draw to

`self` directly without
calling [, the user may see flicker as individual drawing operations are performed in sequence. The clipping and background-initializing features of](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_paint_region)

`begin_paint_region()`[are conveniences for the programmer, so you can avoid doing that work yourself.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_paint_region)

`begin_paint_region()`When using GTK+, the widget system automatically places calls to
[ begin_paint_region()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_paint_region) and

[around emissions of the expose_event signal. That is, if you’re writing an expose event handler, you can assume that the exposed area in](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_paint)

`end_paint()`[has already been cleared to the window background, is already set as the clip region, and already has a backing store. Therefore in most cases, application code need not call](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventExpose.html)

`EventExpose`[. (You can disable the automatic calls around expose events on a widget-by-widget basis by calling](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_paint_region)

`begin_paint_region()``gtk_widget_set_double_buffered()`.)If you call this function multiple times before calling the
matching [ end_paint()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_paint), the backing stores are pushed onto
a stack.

[copies the topmost backing store onscreen, subtracts the topmost region from all other regions in the stack, and pops the stack. All drawing operations affect only the topmost backing store in the stack. One matching call to](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_paint)

`end_paint()`[is required for each call to](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.end_paint)

`end_paint()`[.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_paint_region)

`begin_paint_region()`Use [ begin_draw_frame()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.begin_draw_frame) instead

region you intend to draw to

`thaw_updates()`[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/window.rs.html#567-571)#### pub fn [fullscreen](https://gtk-rs.org#method.fullscreen)(&self)

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/window.rs.html#567-571)

#### pub fn [fullscreen](https://gtk-rs.org#method.fullscreen)(&self)

Moves the window into fullscreen mode. This means the window covers the entire screen and is above any panels or task bars.

If the window was already fullscreen, then this function does nothing.

On X11, asks the window manager to put `self` in a fullscreen
state, if the window manager supports this operation. Not all
window managers support this, and some deliberately ignore it or
don’t have a concept of “fullscreen”; so you can’t rely on the
fullscreenification actually happening. But it will happen with
most standard window managers, and GDK makes a best effort to get
it to happen.

#### pub fn [scale_factor](https://gtk-rs.org#method.scale_factor)(&self) -> [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)

Returns the internal scale factor that maps from window coordiantes to the actual device pixels. On traditional systems this is 1, but on very high density outputs this can be a higher value (often 2).

A higher value means that drawing is automatically scaled up to a higher resolution, so any code doing drawing will automatically look nicer. However, if you are supplying pixel-based data the scale value can be used to determine whether to use a pixel resource with higher resolution data.

The scale of a window may change during runtime, if this happens a configure event will be sent to the toplevel window.

the scale factor

`v3_24`Moves `self` to `rect`, aligning their anchor points.

`rect` is relative to the top-left corner of the window that `self` is
transient for. `rect_anchor` and `window_anchor` determine anchor points on
`rect` and `self` to pin together. `rect`’s anchor point can optionally be
offset by `rect_anchor_dx` and `rect_anchor_dy`, which is equivalent to
offsetting the position of `self`.

`anchor_hints` determines how `self` will be moved if the anchor points cause
it to move off-screen. For example, [ AnchorHints::FLIP_X](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.AnchorHints.html#associatedconstant.FLIP_X) will replace

[with](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.Gravity.html#variant.NorthWest)

`Gravity::NorthWest`[and vice versa if](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.Gravity.html#variant.NorthEast)

`Gravity::NorthEast``self` extends beyond the left or right edges of the monitor.Connect to the `signal::Window::moved-to-rect` signal to find out how it was
actually positioned.

with opacity 0 being fully transparent and 1 fully opaque. (Values
of the opacity parameter are clamped to the [0,1] range.)

For toplevel windows this depends on support from the windowing system
that may not always be there. For instance, On X11, this works only on
X screens with a compositing manager running. On Wayland, there is no
per-window opacity value that the compositor would apply. Instead, use
`gdk_window_set_opaque_region (window, NULL)` to tell the compositor
that the entire window is (potentially) non-opaque, and draw your content
with alpha, or use `gtk_widget_set_opacity()` to set an overall opacity
for your widgets.

For child windows this function only works for non-native windows.

For setting up per-pixel alpha topelevels, see [ Screen::rgba_visual()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Screen.html#method.rgba_visual),
and for non-toplevels, see

`gdk_window_set_composited()`.Support for non-toplevel windows was added in 3.8.

opacity

This function only works for toplevel windows.

the `self` background is opaque, as we know where the opaque regions

property in your `GtkWidget::style-updated` handler.

a region, or `None`

An override redirect window is not under the control of the window manager. This means it won’t have a titlebar, won’t be minimizable, etc. - it will be entirely under the control of the application. The window manager can’t see the override redirect window at all.

Override redirect should only be used for short-lived temporary
windows, such as popup menus. `GtkMenu` uses an override redirect
window in its implementation, for example.

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/window.rs.html#2450-2454)#### pub fn [set_pass_through](https://gtk-rs.org#method.set_pass_through)(&self, pass_through: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/window.rs.html#2450-2454)

#### pub fn [set_pass_through](https://gtk-rs.org#method.set_pass_through)(&self, pass_through: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Sets whether input to the window is passed through to the window below.

The default value of this is [ false](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), which means that pointer
events that happen inside the window are send first to the window,
but if the event is not selected by the event mask then the event
is sent to the parent window, and so on up the hierarchy.

If `pass_through` is [ true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) then such pointer events happen as if the
window wasn’t there at all, and thus will be sent first to any
windows below

`self`. This is useful if the window is used in a
transparent fashion. In the terminology of the web this would be called
“pointer-events: none”.Note that a window with `pass_through` [ true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) can still have a subwindow
without pass through, so you can get events on a subset of a window. And in
that cases you would get the in-between related events such as the pointer
enter/leave events on its way to the destination window.

a boolean

When using GTK+, typically you should use `gtk_window_set_role()` instead
of this low-level function.

The window manager and session manager use a window’s role to distinguish it from other kinds of window in the same application. When an application is restarted after being saved in a previous session, all windows with the same title and role are treated as interchangeable. So if you have two windows with the same title that should be distinguished for session management purposes, you should set the role on those windows. It doesn’t matter what string you use for the role, as long as you have a different role for each non-interchangeable kind of window.

a string indicating its role

Newer GTK+ windows using client-side decorations use extra geometry around their frames for effects like shadows and invisible borders. Window managers that want to maximize windows or snap to edges need to know where the extents of the actual frame lie, so that users don’t feel like windows are snapping against random invisible edges.

Note that this property is automatically updated by GTK+, so this function should only be used by applications which do not use GTK+ to create toplevel windows.

The left extent

The right extent

The top extent

The bottom extent

Moves the window out of fullscreen mode. If the window was not fullscreen, does nothing.

On X11, asks the window manager to move `self` out of the fullscreen
state, if the window manager supports this operation. Not all
window managers support this, and some deliberately ignore it or
don’t have a concept of “fullscreen”; so you can’t rely on the
unfullscreenification actually happening. But it will happen with
most standard window managers, and GDK makes a best effort to get
it to happen.

With update debugging enabled, calls to
[ invalidate_region()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.invalidate_region) clear the invalidated region of the
screen to a noticeable color, and GDK pauses for a short time
before sending exposes to windows during

[. The net effect is that you can see the invalid region for each window and watch redraws as they occur. This allows you to diagnose inefficiencies in your application.](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.process_updates)

`process_updates()`In essence, because the GDK rendering model prevents all flicker, if you are redrawing the same region 400 times you may never notice, aside from noticing a speed problem. Enabling update debugging causes GTK to flicker slowly and noticeably, so you can see exactly what’s being redrawn when, in what order.

The –gtk-debug=updates command line option passed to GTK+ programs
enables this debug option at application startup time. That’s
usually more useful than calling [ set_debug_updates()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.set_debug_updates)
yourself, though you might want to use this function to enable
updates sometime after application startup time.

[ true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) to turn on update debugging

Create a new surface that is as compatible as possible with the
given `self`. For example the new surface will have the same
fallback resolution and font options as `self`. Generally, the new
surface will also use the same backend as `self`, unless that is
not possible for some reason. The type of the returned surface may
be examined with `cairo_surface_get_type()`.

Initially the surface contents are all 0 (transparent if contents have transparency, black otherwise.)

the content for the new surface

width of the new surface

height of the new surface

a pointer to the newly allocated surface. The caller
owns the surface and should call `cairo_surface_destroy()` when done
with it.

This function always returns a valid pointer, but it will return a
pointer to a “nil” surface if `other` is already in an error state
or any other error occurs.

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/window.rs.html#236-252)

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/window.rs.html#236-252)

Create a new image surface that is efficient to draw on the
given `self`.

Initially the surface contents are all 0 (transparent if contents have transparency, black otherwise.)

The `width` and `height` of the new surface are not affected by
the scaling factor of the `self`, or by the `scale` argument; they
are the size of the surface in device pixels. If you wish to create
an image surface capable of holding the contents of `self` you can
use:

**⚠️ The following code is in C ⚠️**

```
  int scale = gdk_window_get_scale_factor (window);
  int width = gdk_window_get_width (window) * scale;
  int height = gdk_window_get_height (window) * scale;
  // format is set elsewhere
  cairo_surface_t *surface =
    gdk_window_create_similar_image_surface (window,
                                             format,
                                             width, height,
                                             scale);
```
Note that unlike `cairo_surface_create_similar_image()`, the new
surface’s device scale is set to `scale`, or to the scale factor of
`self` if `scale` is 0.

the format for the new surface

width of the new surface

height of the new surface

the scale of the new surface, or 0 to use same as `self`

a pointer to the newly allocated surface. The caller
owns the surface and should call `cairo_surface_destroy()` when done
with it.

This function always returns a valid pointer, but it will return a
pointer to a “nil” surface if `other` is already in an error state
or any other error occurs.

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/src/glib/object.rs.html#2770)#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/src/glib/object.rs.html#2770)

#### fn [watch_closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/object/trait.ObjectExt.html#tymethod.watch_closure)(&self, closure: &impl [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Closure](https://gtk-rs.org/gtk-rs-core/stable/0.15/docs/glib/closure/struct.Closure.html)>)

Limits the lifetime of `closure` to the lifetime of the object. When
the object’s reference count drops to zero, the closure will be
invalidated. An invalidated closure will ignore any calls to
[ Closure::invoke](crate::Closure::invoke).

# EventButton in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.EventButton.html

`pub struct EventButton(_);`## Expand description

Used for button press and button release events. The
`type` field will be one of [ EventType::ButtonPress](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ButtonPress),
[

`EventType::_2buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_2buttonPress], [`EventType::_3buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_3buttonPress] or [,](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ButtonRelease)

`EventType::ButtonRelease`Double and triple-clicks result in a sequence of events being received. For double-clicks the order of events will be:

- `EventType::ButtonPress`
- `EventType::ButtonRelease`
- `EventType::ButtonPress`
- [`EventType::_2buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_2buttonPress]
- `EventType::ButtonRelease`

Note that the first click is received just like a normal
button press, while the second click results in a [`EventType::_2buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_2buttonPress]
being received just after the [ EventType::ButtonPress](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.ButtonPress).

Triple-clicks are very similar to double-clicks, except that
[`EventType::_3buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_3buttonPress] is inserted after the third click. The order of the
events is:

- `EventType::ButtonPress`
- `EventType::ButtonRelease`
- `EventType::ButtonPress`
- [`EventType::_2buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_2buttonPress]
- `EventType::ButtonRelease`
- `EventType::ButtonPress`
- [`EventType::_3buttonPress`][crate::EventType::_3buttonPress]
- `EventType::ButtonRelease`

For a double click to occur, the second button press must occur within 1/4 of a second of the first. For a triple click to occur, the third button press must also occur within 1/2 second of the first button press.

Specifies the type of the event.

Do not confuse these events with the signals that GTK+ widgets emit. Although many of these events result in corresponding signals being emitted, the events are often transformed or filtered along the way.

In some language bindings, the values [`_2buttonPress`][Self::_2buttonPress] and
[`_3buttonPress`][Self::_3buttonPress] would translate into something syntactically
invalid (eg `Gdk.EventType.2ButtonPress`, where a
symbol is not allowed to start with a number). In that case, the
aliases [ DoubleButtonPress](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.DoubleButtonPress) and

[can be used instead.](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.TripleButtonPress)

`TripleButtonPress`## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

# EventGrabBroken in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.EventGrabBroken.html

`pub struct EventGrabBroken(_);`## Expand description

Generated when a pointer or keyboard grab is broken. On X11, this happens
when the grab window becomes unviewable (i.e. it or one of its ancestors
is unmapped), or if the same application grabs the pointer or keyboard
again. Note that implicit grabs (which are initiated by button presses)
can also cause [ EventGrabBroken](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventGrabBroken.html) events.

# EventMask in gdk - Rust

Source: https://gtk-rs.org/gtk3-rs/stable/latest/docs/gdk/struct.EventMask.html

`pub struct EventMask { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A set of bit-flags to indicate which events a window is to receive.
Most of these masks map onto one or more of the [ EventType](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html) event types
above.

See the [input handling overview][chap-input-handling] for details of [event masks][event-masks] and [event propagation][event-propagation].

[ POINTER_MOTION_HINT_MASK](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventMask.html#associatedconstant.POINTER_MOTION_HINT_MASK) is deprecated. It is a special mask
to reduce the number of

[events received. When using](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.MotionNotify)

`EventType::MotionNotify`[, fewer](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventMask.html#associatedconstant.POINTER_MOTION_HINT_MASK)

`POINTER_MOTION_HINT_MASK`[events will be sent, some of which are marked as a hint (the is_hint member is](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.MotionNotify)

`EventType::MotionNotify`[). To receive more motion events after a motion hint event, the application needs to asks for more, by calling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`true``gdk_event_request_motions()`.Since GTK 3.8, motion events are already compressed by default, independent
of this mechanism. This compression can be disabled with
[ Window::set_event_compression()](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.Window.html#method.set_event_compression). See the documentation of that function
for details.

If [ TOUCH_MASK](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventMask.html#associatedconstant.TOUCH_MASK) is enabled, the window will receive touch events
from touch-enabled devices. Those will come as sequences of

[with type](https://gtk-rs.org/struct.EventTouch.html)

`EventTouch`[, enclosed by two events with type](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.TouchUpdate)

`EventType::TouchUpdate`[and](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.TouchBegin)

`EventType::TouchBegin`[(or](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.TouchEnd)

`EventType::TouchEnd`[).](https://gtk-rs.org/enum.EventType.html#variant.TouchCancel)

`EventType::TouchCancel``gdk_event_get_event_sequence()` returns the event sequence for these
events, so different sequences may be distinguished.[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/flags.rs.html#324-433)#### pub const [EXPOSURE_MASK](https://gtk-rs.org#associatedconstant.EXPOSURE_MASK): Self = Self{bits: ffi::GDK_EXPOSURE_MASK as u32,}

[source](https://gtk-rs.org/src/gdk/auto/flags.rs.html#324-433)

#### pub const [EXPOSURE_MASK](https://gtk-rs.org#associatedconstant.EXPOSURE_MASK): Self = Self{bits: ffi::GDK_EXPOSURE_MASK as u32,}

receive expose events

Convert from underlying bit representation, preserving all bits (even those not corresponding to a defined flag).

The caller of the `bitflags!` macro can chose to allow or
disallow extra bits for their bitflags type.

The caller of `from_bits_unchecked()` has to ensure that
all bits correspond to a defined flag or that extra bits
are valid for this bitflags type.
